translations.title: Maintaining Your Identity
translations.explanation: Learning goal: derive and use special-angle values and trigonometric symmetries from the unit circle (CCSS HSF-TF.A.3 and A.4). Angles in this lesson are in radians unless explicitly marked in degrees. For an angle θ, the point on the unit circle is (cos θ, sin θ); when cos θ ≠ 0, tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. Reflecting or rotating that point changes its coordinates predictably. The coordinates, rather than a remembered mnemonic, explain why sine is odd, cosine is even, and the functions repeat after a full revolution. The identities here hold for every real θ at which the expressions are defined. The related identity sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 follows from the unit circle and helps check a result.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
From a 30°–60°–90° triangle, sin(π/6) = 1/2, cos(π/6) = √3/2 and tan(π/6) = 1/√3; reversing the acute angles gives the π/3 values. From an isosceles right triangle, sin(π/4) = cos(π/4) = √2/2 and tan(π/4) = 1. Unit-circle reflection: sin(π−θ) = sin θ, cos(π−θ) = −cos θ; rotation: sin(π+θ) = −sin θ, cos(π+θ) = −cos θ; full-turn reflection: sin(2π−θ) = −sin θ, cos(2π−θ) = cos θ. Divide sine by cosine to obtain the corresponding tangent relations only when both tangent expressions exist. Parity: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ where defined. Periodicity: sin(θ+2π) = sin θ, cos(θ+2π) = cos θ and tan(θ+π) = tan θ when defined. Tangent is undefined at θ = π/2 + kπ for integer k.

Cofunction identity: sin θ = cos(π/2−θ) for every real θ. It follows by exchanging the horizontal and vertical legs in a right triangle (for acute θ) and by reflecting corresponding coordinates on the unit circle (for every angle). The Pythagorean identity sin² θ+cos² θ=1 is the equation x²+y²=1 applied to (cos θ,sin θ).
translations.workedExamples:
Example A — special triangle. The shorter leg of a 30°–60°–90° triangle is 1, the longer leg is √3 and hypotenuse is 2. Thus the unit-circle point at π/6 is (√3/2, 1/2). Example B — reflections. Take θ = π/6. The unit-circle point for π−θ = 5π/6 is (−√3/2, 1/2); hence sin(5π/6) = 1/2, cos(5π/6) = −√3/2, tan(5π/6) = −1/√3. Example C — rotation. π+π/6 = 7π/6, so its sine is −1/2 and cosine is −√3/2. Example D — a full-turn reflection. 2π−π/6 = 11π/6, giving sin = −1/2, cos = √3/2 and tan = −1/√3. All four results follow from the coordinate transformations, not approximation.

Example E — verified cofunction bridge to the original geometry task. A 30°–60°–90° triangle shows sin(π/6)=1/2=cos(π/3)=cos(π/2−π/6). On the unit circle, the complementary angle exchanges the sine and cosine coordinates. This is a relationship between functions for any angle, not only acute angles.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Task: explain why cos(π−θ) = −cos θ and sin(π−θ) = sin θ, then evaluate sin(5π/6), cos(5π/6), and tan(5π/6). Step 1: mark (cos θ, sin θ) on the unit circle. Step 2: reflect that point across the y-axis; its new coordinates are (−cos θ, sin θ), and its angle is π−θ modulo 2π. Step 3: identify the sine as the y-coordinate and cosine as the x-coordinate; the two identities follow. Step 4: a 30°–60°–90° triangle gives sin(π/6)=1/2 and cos(π/6)=√3/2. Step 5: substitute θ=π/6: sin(5π/6)=1/2, cos(5π/6)=−√3/2, tan(5π/6)=(1/2)/(−√3/2)=−1/√3. Step 6: check 1/4+3/4=1 and the second-quadrant signs. Independent check: substituting θ=π/2 into the sine/cosine identities yields the correct unit-circle point; tangent is excluded where cosine is zero.

Additional diagram-free proof task: derive sin θ=cos(π/2−θ). Reflect the unit-circle point (cos θ,sin θ) across the diagonal y=x to obtain (sin θ,cos θ), the point at angle π/2−θ; therefore cos(π/2−θ)=sin θ. Check the reflection identity at θ=π/6 and θ=7π/6 to avoid arguing from acute triangles alone.

Accessible unit-circle construction (first-party, text alternative): Take axes with right=positive x and up=positive y. At θ=π/6, mark P=(√3/2,1/2). Reflect P over the y-axis to obtain Q=(−√3/2,1/2) at 5π/6. Rotate P half a turn to R=(−√3/2,−1/2) at 7π/6; reflect P over the x-axis to T=(√3/2,−1/2) at 11π/6. For each point report its quadrant, cosine (x), sine (y), and tangent (y/x). A student not using a visual diagram can identify each point by its ordered pair and named sign changes. Explain why P and Q have the same y coordinate and opposite x coordinates; give a general coordinate-reflection argument rather than treating these four values as a proof for all angles.

Source-aligned conjecture check and accessible graph-equivalent table (student investigation, not a proof). Compare six pairs of expressions for any angle x: sin(π−x) against sin x; cos(π−x) against −cos x; sin(π+x) against −sin x; cos(π+x) against −cos x; sin(2π−x) against −sin x; and cos(2π−x) against cos x. Plot each pair over [−2π,2π] if graphing is available. For nonvisual access, use a table with columns x, transformed angle, both function values and the signed coordinate change; include x=π/6 and x=7π/6. Identical plotted curves or a finite table provide supporting evidence only: to establish each identity for every real x, prove the corresponding reflection or half-turn transformation of (cos x,sin x) on the unit circle.

Algebraic tangent proof (source task follow-up). If cos x≠0, tan(−x)=sin(−x)/cos(−x)=(−sin x)/(cos x)=−tan x. Under the same condition, tan(π+x)=sin(π+x)/cos(π+x)=(−sin x)/(−cos x)=tan x. At x=π/2+kπ, for any integer k, tangent expressions are undefined, so neither quotient proof may claim a value at a pole. This is an algebraic derivation using sine/cosine identities, not a graph-based proof.

Check for understanding — learner response. (1) Evaluate cos(π−π/3) and sin(π+π/3) exactly and explain each quadrant sign. (2) Starting with tan x=sin x/cos x, prove tan(π+x)=tan x for general permissible x and state its domain. (3) Decide whether tan(π/2) can be evaluated and why. (4) Describe the reflection of the generic point (cos x,sin x) across the y-axis, and explain why one numerical example or coincident-looking graphs cannot prove an identity. Answer key: (1) −1/2 and −√3/2, respectively; (2) both sine and cosine change sign, so their quotient stays equal if cos x≠0; (3) undefined because the denominator is zero; (4) (−cos x,sin x), corresponding to π−x modulo 2π. Score the arbitrary-angle reasoning and domain under the existing L01 six-point HUMAN_REQUIRED rubric; do not award proof credit for a numeric-only answer.

Text-first right-triangle construction for the original acute-angle argument (no publisher figure): Draw triangle ABC with a right angle at A, angle B=x, angle C=90°−x, hypotenuse BC=h, and legs AC=a, AB=b. At B, sin(x)=a/h. At C, cos(90°−x)=a/h because AC is adjacent to angle C. This is an equality of side ratios for EVERY 0°<x<90°, not just the special-angle check a=1, b=sqrt(3), h=2 at x=30°. This triangle is not a proof outside the acute interval; for all real x use the unit-circle point P=(cos x,sin x), whose reflection across y=x is P'=(sin x,cos x) at pi/2−x. The text description, angle labels and ordered pairs remain usable without viewing a drawing.

Two worked sample rows for all six conjectures (radians; every value exact, and accessible independently of a plot). Columns: base angle x | (sin x,cos x) | pi−x : (sin,cos) | pi+x : (sin,cos) | 2pi−x : (sin,cos).
Row 1: x=pi/6 | (1/2,sqrt(3)/2) | 5pi/6 : (1/2,-sqrt(3)/2) | 7pi/6 : (-1/2,-sqrt(3)/2) | 11pi/6 : (-1/2,sqrt(3)/2).
Row 2: x=7pi/6 | (-1/2,-sqrt(3)/2) | -pi/6 : (-1/2,sqrt(3)/2) | 13pi/6 : (1/2,sqrt(3)/2) | 5pi/6 : (1/2,-sqrt(3)/2).
For a plot or nonvisual graph-table exploration, compare six pairs of plotted values: (sin(pi−x),sin x), (cos(pi−x),−cos x), (sin(pi+x),−sin x), (cos(pi+x),−cos x), (sin(2pi−x),−sin x), and (cos(2pi−x),cos x) over x in [-2pi,2pi]; these are ordered comparisons, not quotients. Ask learners to identify the reflection/half-turn corresponding to each pair. Equal sample values or coincident curves are evidence for a conjecture, NOT proof for all real x; justify by the generic coordinate transformations above. The six-point human rubric grades reasoning and tangent-domain statements separately from exact numeric Practice.
translations.commonMistakes: Confusing a reflected point's x- and y-coordinates: a reflection across the y-axis changes cosine's sign, not sine's. Treating tangent as defined when cos θ=0: quotient identities must exclude θ=π/2+kπ. Writing tan(θ+2π) as the only tangent period: π is the fundamental period, although 2π also works. Treating sin(−θ)=sin θ: sine is odd, while cosine is even. Applying degree-mode calculator values to radian expressions: π/6 rad = 30°, not 0.5236°. Claiming a numerical example proves an identity: prove the coordinate transformation first, then use values as checks.
translations.quickSummary: On the unit circle, (cos θ, sin θ) gives every trigonometric value. Special right triangles determine exact values at π/6, π/4 and π/3. Reflection and rotation derive the identities for π−θ, π+θ and 2π−θ. Cosine is even; sine and tangent are odd wherever defined. Sine and cosine repeat every 2π; tangent repeats every π and is undefined when cosine is zero. Check each transformed value by quadrant signs and sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.

translations.title: The Amazing Inverse Trig Function Race
translations.explanation: Learning goal: construct inverse trigonometric functions by restricting sine, cosine and tangent to one-to-one intervals (CCSS HSF-TF.B.6). The full sine, cosine and tangent graphs repeat values, so their unrestricted inverses are not functions. Choose intervals where each function is strictly monotonic, then exchange input and output to construct its inverse. We write arcsin u, arccos u and arctan u (also sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹); the superscript −1 here means inverse function, not reciprocal. One principal-value answer represents an angle in a specified interval, NOT all angles with that trigonometric value. Use radians unless degrees are explicitly requested, and verify outputs by composing with the original function on its restricted domain.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Sine is one-to-one on [−π/2, π/2] with range [−1,1]; arcsin has domain [−1,1] and range [−π/2,π/2]. Cosine is one-to-one on [0,π] with range [−1,1]; arccos has domain [−1,1] and range [0,π]. Tangent is one-to-one on (−π/2,π/2), with range all real values; arctan has domain all real numbers and range (−π/2,π/2). For u in [−1,1], sin(arcsin u)=u and cos(arccos u)=u. For every real u, tan(arctan u)=u. The reverse compositions arcsin(sin θ)=θ, arccos(cos θ)=θ, arctan(tan θ)=θ only when θ belongs to the specified principal range and, for tangent, is not at an asymptote. The full sine-equation solution uses α=arcsin u and θ=α+2kπ or θ=π−α+2kπ (k integer). Reject |u|>1 for real inverse sine/cosine.
translations.workedExamples:
Example A: arcsin(√3/2)=π/3 because sin(π/3)=√3/2 and π/3 lies in [−π/2,π/2]. Example B: arccos(−1/2)=2π/3 because cos(2π/3)=−1/2 and 2π/3 lies in [0,π]. Example C: arctan(−1)=−π/4, not 3π/4, because the principal arctangent range is (−π/2,π/2). Example D: arcsin(sin(5π/6))=π/6, NOT 5π/6: both angles share sine 1/2, but only π/6 is in the chosen inverse range. Example E: cos θ=1/2 for 0≤θ<2π has θ=π/3 and θ=5π/3; arccos returns π/3 as the reference principal angle, and unit-circle symmetry supplies the other solution.

Example F — original-source-inspired two-clue location reasoning, independently written. An angle clue says sin θ=1/2 and a second clue says the location is in quadrant II at distance 2 units from the origin. The inverse sine returns π/6, but the quadrant constraint selects θ=5π/6. Therefore the unique Cartesian coordinate is (−√3,1). If the second clue instead said that y<0, the clues would contradict one another; a valid grader must not invent a location.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Task: solve sin θ=1/2 on the interval 0≤θ<2π, explaining why arcsin gives only one of the answers. Step 1: note −1≤1/2≤1, so a real inverse sine exists. Step 2: compute α=arcsin(1/2)=π/6 using the special triangle and verify α belongs to [−π/2,π/2]. Step 3: sine is positive in quadrants I and II; the second angle is π−α=5π/6. Step 4: check sin(π/6)=1/2 and sin(5π/6)=1/2. Step 5: both angles are in [0,2π); no other solutions occur in one full revolution. Step 6: explain that sin is many-to-one before restriction, so arcsin(sin(5π/6))=π/6. Technology check: set a calculator to radian mode; graph y=sin θ and y=1/2 for 0≤θ<2π, then compare intersections with exact solutions.

Two-clue reasoning: Step 1 find principal α=arcsin(1/2)=π/6. Step 2 enumerate angles with the given sine on [0,2π): π/6 and 5π/6. Step 3 apply the quadrant II clue and keep 5π/6. Step 4 multiply unit-circle coordinates by radius 2 to obtain (−√3,1). Step 5 reject any contradictory coordinate clue rather than forcing an inverse function to return an impossible location. A source-inspired exploration of uniqueness is distinct from copying the original activity cards.

Source-inspired inverse graph and location race (first-party accessible alternative): Describe or plot these ordered angle/value pairs in increasing angle order: sine (−π/2,−1), (0,0), (π/2,1); cosine (0,1), (π/2,0), (π,−1); tangent (−π/4,−1), (0,0), (π/4,1). State which restricted graph rises or falls and why the chosen interval is one-to-one (the three points are checkpoints, not a proof of monotonicity). For the clue sin θ=1/2 on [0,2π), report both candidate locations π/6 and 5π/6; a quadrant-II clue makes the answer unique, no quadrant clue leaves two answers, and a y<0 clue makes the clues inconsistent. State the principal arcsin output π/6 separately from the selected physical location; an accessible written response is equivalent to marking the positions on a grid.

Source task 7.8H — three independent first-party game rounds (angle clue + location clue), with an accessible choice of Cartesian or polar coordinates. Round 1: angle clue sin θ=1/2, 0≤θ<2π; location clue radius r=2 and quadrant II. The possible sine angles are π/6 and 5π/6, but only 5π/6 meets the quadrant clue; the unique stake position is (−√3,1), or (r,θ)=(2,5π/6). Round 2: the same angle clue with only radius r=2. Both (√3,1) and (−√3,1) are possible; mark both, not an invented unique point. Round 3: sin θ=1/2 with a proposed location y=−1 for positive radius. These clues are contradictory because y=r sin θ>0 whenever r>0. For each round, record clues, the set of admissible positions, and whether it is unique/multiple/impossible. Explain how additional independent information can select one solution rather than assuming two clues always suffice.

Original 0.75 inverse-sine graph investigation (independently authored response): Let α=arcsin(0.75)≈0.84806207898 radians. Other angles with sin θ=0.75 include π−α≈2.29353057461, α+2π≈7.13124738616, and 3π−α≈8.57671588179. The principal inverse output α is not the set of all sine-equation roots. Show the matching input/value pairs on a graph or in an accessible ordered table. For the inverse graph, restrict sin to [−π/2,π/2] and reflect its monotone graph in y=x; explain why the reflected relation is a single-valued function. Repeat with cos on [0,π] (strictly decreasing) and tan on (−π/2,π/2) (strictly increasing with excluded poles). Check for understanding: arcsin(−1/2)=−π/6; arccos(−1/2)=2π/3; arctan(1)=π/4, all in radians. Justify every principal branch and reject arcsin(1.2), arccos(−1.2) and any arctan output ±π/2. These checks complement, not reproduce, publisher cards or diagrams.
translations.commonMistakes: Confusing sin⁻¹ u with 1/sin u: use arcsin for the inverse and csc for the reciprocal. Reporting every original θ after applying arcsin(sin θ): the output is always in [−π/2,π/2]. Omitting the second solution to a trigonometric equation because the inverse gives one principal value. Entering arcsin(2) or arccos(−1.3) in the real-number domain. Switching radians and degrees halfway through a solution. Including ±π/2 as tangent-inverse outputs: arctan never reaches those asymptotic values. Claiming any arbitrary interval defines the standard inverse: the chosen interval must be one-to-one and its range must match the desired inverse domain.
translations.quickSummary: A periodic trigonometric function is not globally one-to-one. Restrict sine to [−π/2,π/2], cosine to [0,π] and tangent to (−π/2,π/2) to define arcsin, arccos and arctan. Their outputs are principal angles; composing an inverse with a trig function does not generally recover an unrestricted original angle. For equations over a larger interval, use the unit circle and periodicity to find all solutions, then check the required interval and calculator angle mode.

translations.title: Hidden Identities
translations.explanation: Learning goal: use trigonometric identities together with inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations, enumerate all solutions in a stated interval, and interpret a modeling result (CCSS HSF-TF.B.7). An identity changes the form of an expression without changing its value where it is defined. For example, cos(π/2−θ)=sin θ follows from the unit circle. This can turn an unfamiliar cosine equation into a familiar sine equation. Inverse sine or inverse cosine produces a principal angle; periodicity and symmetry produce other valid angles. In applications, translate the angles back to elapsed time, location or another quantity, reject results outside the physical domain and check them in the original equation. A graph or numerical calculation is a second check, not a substitute for the algebra.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Useful identities: cos(π/2−θ)=sin θ, sin(π/2−θ)=cos θ, sin² θ+cos² θ=1, sin(π−θ)=sin θ, cos(−θ)=cos θ. Given sin θ=u with |u|≤1, let α=arcsin u in [−π/2,π/2]; solutions are θ=α+2kπ or θ=π−α+2kπ for integer k. Given cos θ=u with |u|≤1, β=arccos u in [0,π]; solutions are θ=±β+2kπ. For tan θ=u, γ=arctan u, solutions are θ=γ+kπ, excluding tangent poles. These formulas generate candidates: keep only solutions in the stated interval, in radian or degree units consistently, and check the original equation for domain restrictions or extraneous roots. A model equation also requires interpreting units, physical bounds and possibly multiple times within a cycle.
translations.workedExamples:
Example A — Hidden identity. Solve cos(π/2−θ)=1/2 on [0,2π]. Replace cos(π/2−θ) with sin θ to obtain sin θ=1/2. The principal angle is arcsin(1/2)=π/6; the second-quadrant angle is π−π/6=5π/6. Both satisfy the original cosine equation. Example B — periodic modeling. A rotating beacon has signal S(t)=10+4 sin(πt/6), where t is measured in seconds and 0≤t<12. Signal 12 means sin(πt/6)=1/2. Because πt/6 traverses [0,2π), the solutions are t=1 and t=5 seconds. Verify S(1)=S(5)=12. Example C — a restricted domain. If the beacon operates only during 0≤t≤3 seconds, keep t=1 and discard t=5; the physical constraint matters.

Example F — compressed-period source-type check. Solve sin(2θ)=√3/2 for 0≤θ<2π. Let u=2θ; then 0≤u<4π. In two revolutions u=π/3, 2π/3, 7π/3, 8π/3. Halving gives θ=π/6, π/3, 7π/6, 4π/3. Substitution confirms all four. Finding only two angles would miss the second revolution.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Task: determine every θ in [0,2π] satisfying cos(π/2−θ)=1/2, then explain why an inverse calculator alone is insufficient. Step 1: use cos(π/2−θ)=sin θ, so sin θ=1/2. Step 2: obtain α=arcsin(1/2)=π/6. Step 3: add the equal-sine angle π−α=5π/6. Step 4: check endpoints: θ=0 and θ=2π give cos(π/2)=0, not 1/2, so the solutions are exactly π/6 and 5π/6. Step 5: directly substitute: cos(π/3)=1/2 at θ=π/6, and cos(−π/3)=1/2 at θ=5π/6. Step 6: graph y=cos(π/2−θ) and y=1/2 on [0,2π] in radian mode and identify both intersections. Step 7: in a timing model θ=πt/6, multiply each angle by 6/π to obtain t=1,5 seconds, then check each falls within the permitted time interval.

Compare three strategies for cos(π/2−θ)=1/2 over [0,2π]: (i) let u=π/2−θ and solve cos u=1/2 with inverse cosine and the correct transformed interval; (ii) rewrite as sin θ=1/2 using the cofunction identity, then add the symmetric angle; (iii) find both intersections of y=cos(π/2−θ) with y=1/2 on a radian-mode graph. All three yield π/6 and 5π/6. For sin(2θ)=√3/2, account for two cycles in 2θ; there are four θ solutions, not two.

Accessible graph/technology investigation (first-party student task): On 0≤θ<2π, graph or tabulate the two functions y₁=sin(2θ) and y₂=√3/2 with horizontal axis θ in radians. Enumerate all four intersections θ=π/6, π/3, 7π/6, 4π/3 and check each against the ORIGINAL equation; show why one period of sin θ would miss two answers. Check 0 and 2π as excluded nonroots. For the separate Edulytiks-authored beacon model, graph S(t)=10+4sin(πt/6) and y=12 for 0≤t<12 seconds, and report intersections t=1,5 seconds with units and physical interval. Describe every graph intersection as an ordered input/output pair for learners who cannot use a visual plot. This beacon context is not presented as the publisher’s original equation task.

Original 7.6 identity-based practice, independently written: on 0≤θ≤2π, solve (1) sin(−θ)=−√3/2 by applying odd parity to obtain sin θ=√3/2, hence θ=π/3 or 2π/3. The minus sign inside sine is not simply cancelled: the identity sin(−θ)=−sin θ is the necessary justification. (2) Solve cos θ·tan θ=√3/2: first require cos θ≠0, then replace tan θ by sin θ/cos θ, reducing to sin θ=√3/2. The same two answers work in the original expression; poles θ=π/2 and 3π/2 are forbidden, not additional solutions. (3) Solve sin(2θ)=√3/2: because u=2θ covers [0,4π], the four answers are θ=π/6, π/3, 7π/6, 4π/3. On this task neither 0 nor 2π solves the equations. Compare Alyce's inverse-cosine substitution, Javier's identity-first inverse sine and Veronica's graphical/table root enumeration. A calculator's principal inverse alone is not an exhaustive solution method. An accessible technology check reports all intersections as ordered pairs (θ, function value) with the interval and angular units. These source-equation tasks remain distinct from the independently authored beacon-time real-world model. Check for understanding: explain the role of odd symmetry, the domain cancellation, why the doubled angle traverses two revolutions and why isolated plotted points do not establish completeness. The general proof and technology/context interpretation require human evaluation.
translations.commonMistakes: Assuming θ=arcsin(u) is the only solution on an entire period; sine usually has two distinct angles. Using an identity with the wrong sign, such as cos(π/2−θ)=−sin θ; derive or verify the unit-circle relation. Applying cos⁻¹ or sin⁻¹ while ignoring their principal ranges. Solving for an angle but not converting it back into time or the actual modeled quantity. Keeping an angle that satisfies the transformed expression but lies outside the model's physical interval. Working in degrees while the model's angular rate uses radians. Squaring both sides of an equation and accepting extraneous solutions without checking the original expression.
translations.quickSummary: Use identities to rewrite trigonometric equations, inverse functions to identify reference angles, and unit-circle symmetry plus periodicity to find every solution in the specified interval. An authentic modeling answer must be expressed in the model's units and physical domain. For cos(π/2−θ)=1/2 over one full turn, the valid answers are θ=π/6 and θ=5π/6. Check both by substitution and, when available, technology.

translations.title: Cavelieri to the Rescue
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: explain Cavalieri's principle and use equal-area horizontal cross-sections to justify a volume formula, especially that of a sphere (CCSS HSG-GMD.A.2). Imagine two solids between parallel planes at heights z=0 and z=h. If every horizontal slice of one solid has the same area as the corresponding slice of the other, their volumes are equal. This compares whole volumes without demanding identical exterior shapes. A useful sphere argument compares a hemisphere of radius r with a cylinder of radius r and height r from which an appropriately oriented cone has been removed. We use the established cylinder and cone volume formulas to obtain the sphere formula, explaining the cross-sectional match rather than memorizing the result.

A source-grounded geometric bridge precedes the sphere argument: triangles with the same base and height have the same area even if the apex shifts; likewise, a vertical stack of discs and the same stack sheared sideways occupy equal volumes when each slice has the same area. These investigations illustrate the condition used in Cavalieri’s principle. The sphere calculation that follows is an independently written extension to the source's sphere-volume exploration.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cavalieri's principle: for equal-height solids, if A₁(z)=A₂(z) at every corresponding height 0≤z≤h, then their volumes are equal. Volume has cubic units; each A(z) has square units. In a hemisphere of radius r resting on its equatorial plane, the horizontal circular cross-section at height z (0≤z≤r) has radius √(r²−z²), so area is π(r²−z²). Compare a radius-r, height-r cylinder with a cone removed whose horizontal slice at height z has radius z: the remaining slice also has area πr²−πz². The cylinder volume is πr³; the cone volume is (1/3)πr³. Therefore hemisphere volume is (2/3)πr³ and the full sphere has volume (4/3)πr³. The comparison assumes each solid has the same height and the cone's slice radius really is z; equal bases alone are not enough.
translations.workedExamples:
Example A — sphere derivation. At z=r/2 a radius-r hemisphere slice has area π(r²−r²/4)=3πr²/4. The comparison cylinder has slice πr² and the cone slice π(r/2)²=πr²/4; the difference is the same 3πr²/4. The equality holds for every z, so Cavalieri applies. Example B — numerical volume. For r=3 cm, sphere volume is (4/3)π(3³)=36π cm³, approximately 113.10 cm³. Its hemisphere has 18π cm³. Example C — distinguish volume from area. Two solids may share a base area but differ in how their cross-sectional areas change with height; they need not have equal volumes. Match slice areas at every corresponding height rather than comparing only z=0 or z=h.

Example D — equal-area triangles: two triangles have the same horizontal base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm, but one apex is shifted far to the side. At height z above the base each horizontal slice has length 6(1−z/4), so corresponding slices match for 0≤z≤4; both areas are (1/2)·6·4=12 cm². Example E — right versus oblique circular cylinder: shear a stack of radius-3-cm circular layers sideways without changing their horizontal shapes; at every height 0≤z≤8 cm the slice area is 9π cm², so both volumes are 9π·8=72π cm³. Equal height and cross-sectional AREA, not matching outline, are decisive.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Task: justify V=(4/3)πr³ for a sphere using Cavalieri's principle. Step 1: cut the sphere into two congruent hemispheres along its equator. Step 2: let z measure height above the flat circular base of one hemisphere, so 0≤z≤r. Step 3: by a right triangle in the sphere, the slice radius squared is r²−z² and its area is A_H(z)=π(r²−z²). Step 4: take a cylinder of radius r, height r; remove a cone with apex at z=0 and top base radius r at z=r. By similar triangles, cone slice radius at height z is z. Step 5: the remaining cylinder-minus-cone slice is A_C(z)=πr²−πz²=A_H(z). Step 6: the two solids have the same height, so Cavalieri gives equal volumes. Step 7: V_hemisphere=πr²·r−(1/3)πr²·r=(2/3)πr³. Step 8: double for a full sphere: V_sphere=(4/3)πr³. Step 9: check units are r³, and at r=3 compute 36π cubic units.

Source-specific comparison task: begin with a right radius-3, height-8 cylinder and an oblique cylinder made by translating each horizontal cross-sectional disc sideways. For both solids A(z)=9π square centimeters at every z∈[0,8]. Because heights are equal and corresponding cross-sectional areas are equal, Cavalieri gives equal volumes V=72π cubic centimeters. Distinguish this demonstration from merely checking equal circular bases, which would not prove equal volumes for arbitrary solids.

Every-height cross-section construction (first-party textual alternative): For any r>0 and every z with 0≤z≤r, the hemisphere has A_H(z)=π(r²−z²); the radius-r cylinder with a cone of slice radius z removed has A_C(z)=πr²−πz². Simplify both algebraically to prove A_H(z)=A_C(z) for ALL corresponding z; three sampled heights alone are insufficient for Cavalieri. For r=3 cm, verify the paired values at z=0, 1.5, and 3 cm are respectively 9π, 27π/4, and 0 square centimeters. Describe the slices with words and their formulas instead of relying on a publisher figure. Explain why replacing the cone with a different orientation invalidates the argument, and why an oblique cylinder can preserve area at each height despite its shifted center.

Source 7.12 task-representation investigation (independently authored, no copied diagram): Before measuring, predict whether a skewed, centered or right triangle on common base AB=6 cm and with apex on a parallel line at perpendicular height 4 cm has the largest area. All are 12 cm². A horizontal slice z cm above the base, for 0≤z≤4, has length 6(1−z/4) in every triangle; the slice position shifts but its length does not. Mark or tabulate those segment lengths at z=0,1,2,3,4 to support the area comparison. Make two noncongruent parallelograms with the same 6-cm base and height 4 cm, sliding the top edges horizontally; each has horizontal slice length 6 cm at every height and area 24 cm². For a right and an oblique pyramid sharing perpendicular height h and base area B, similar triangles at height z give corresponding parallel-slice areas A(z)=B(1−z/h)², even though slice centers differ. Cavalieri equates volumes, transferring the established right-pyramid volume Bh/3 to the oblique pyramid; the same argument works for right/oblique cones of equal circular base area and perpendicular height. With B=12 cm² and h=6 cm, both pyramids have volume 24 cm³. A matching base alone or a few sample heights do not establish Cavalieri's every-height requirement. Third-party GeoGebra applets in publisher materials are not copied or claimed to be available. Check for understanding: identify corresponding slices in words or a table; distinguish perpendicular and slanted heights; derive the similarity factor, equal area at every height and cubic units; require a teacher-scored argument rather than an unreasoned volume.
translations.commonMistakes: Claiming equal base areas imply equal volumes; Cavalieri requires matching areas at every corresponding height. Using r²+z² for the hemisphere slice radius squared: the correct Pythagorean relation is sliceRadius²+z²=r². Treating a cross-sectional area as a volume: area is in square units and volume is in cubic units. Comparing the hemisphere with the entire cylinder rather than the cylinder with the cone removed. Assigning the wrong cone orientation and still asserting its slice radius equals z. Forgetting the result gives one hemisphere before multiplying by two. Assuming a drawing establishes equality without explicitly checking cross-section area functions.
translations.quickSummary:
Cavalieri's principle says equal-height solids with equal-area corresponding slices have equal volumes. For 0≤z≤r, a hemisphere slice and a cylinder-minus-cone slice both have area π(r²−z²). Therefore V_hemisphere=πr³−(1/3)πr³=(2/3)πr³, and V_sphere=(4/3)πr³. State the correspondence of slice heights, justify their areas and use cubic volume units.

The original source also demonstrates equal-area noncongruent triangles and equal-volume right and sheared cylinders before extending Cavalieri to sphere, pyramid and cone volumes. A valid argument checks every corresponding slice, not only one or both endpoints.

translations.title: Operating on a Shoestring
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: connect distances to two fixed focal points with the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas (CCSS HSG-GPE.A.3). For a point P=(x,y), the distances to horizontal foci F₁=(−c,0) and F₂=(c,0) are d₁=√((x+c)²+y²) and d₂=√((x−c)²+y²). An ellipse consists of points whose SUM d₁+d₂ is a constant 2a greater than the distance 2c between the foci. A hyperbola consists of points for which the absolute DIFFERENCE |d₁−d₂| is a constant 2a less than 2c. Algebra converts these distance conditions into the standard equations. A loop of taut string fixed at two foci is a useful tactile model for the ellipse; the hyperbola is a related but distinct constant-difference locus. Both derivations below are independent Edulytiks instruction, not a claim of verbatim publisher-task equivalence.

 Source-specific extension to the ellipse exploration: changing the length of a taut loop while keeping the foci fixed changes the constant total focal distance, and moving the foci with constant total focal distance changes the ellipse's width. A vertical focal axis exchanges the roles of x and y; translating both foci changes the center and requires shifted-coordinate equations. These ideas come from the locked 6.10H teacher/student aims, but the examples and calculations here are independently authored.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Distance formula: d((x,y),(u,v))=√((x−u)²+(y−v)²). With foci (±c,0), an ellipse requires a>c≥0, b²=a²−c²>0 and equation x²/a²+y²/b²=1; its vertices are (±a,0) and foci (±c,0). Sum of focal distances equals 2a. With foci (±c,0), a nondegenerate hyperbola requires c>a>0, b²=c²−a²>0 and equation x²/a²−y²/b²=1; its vertices are (±a,0), asymptotes y=±(b/a)x, and absolute difference of focal distances equals 2a. Horizontal examples only: swapping x and y produces analogous vertical axes. If a=c in an ellipse or a=c in the hyperbola, the standard nondegenerate formulas cease to apply; check the strict inequalities before dividing by b². If solving squared distance equations, check candidates against the original nonnegative distances and required sum/difference.

 Vertical-axis formulas: for ellipse foci (0,±c), use x²/b²+y²/a²=1 with a>c and b²=a²−c². For hyperbola foci (0,±c), use y²/a²−x²/b²=1 with c>a and b²=c²−a². For a translated ellipse centered at (h,k) with horizontal foci (h±c,k), use (x−h)²/a²+(y−k)²/b²=1. With fixed c, increasing a also increases b; with fixed a, increasing c decreases b, so the ellipse becomes narrower. Keep track of whether the axis of larger denominator is horizontal or vertical.
translations.workedExamples:
Example A — ellipse from foci and string. Foci F₁=(−3,0), F₂=(3,0); a two-ended string stretched from the foci via a pencil has length 10, while a taut closed loop running around both tacks and the pencil has physical length 16 (10 focal-distance sum plus the fixed 6-unit tack-to-tack return segment). Then 2a=10, a=5, c=3, b²=25−9=16. Equation: x²/25+y²/16=1. At vertex (5,0), focal distances are 8 and 2, summing to 10; at (0,4), both distances are 5. Example B — hyperbola from foci. Foci (−5,0),(5,0); absolute difference of distances is 6. Then a=3, c=5 and b²=25−9=16. Equation: x²/9−y²/16=1. At vertex (3,0), focal distances are 8 and 2, differing by 6. Example C — distinguish the constraints. With foci ±3, an ellipse with distance sum 4 is impossible because 4 is less than focal separation 6. With foci ±5, a hyperbola with focal-distance difference 12 is impossible because it exceeds separation 10.

 Example D — compare string/focal effects. With fixed foci (−3,0),(3,0), a=5 gives x²/25+y²/16=1, while a=6 gives x²/36+y²/27=1: the new figure extends farther along its major axis and also widens. With fixed a=5 but foci (±4,0), b²=25−16=9: the ellipse is narrower than with c=3. Example E — vertical axis. Foci (0,−3),(0,3), distance sum 10 give x²/16+y²/25=1. The point (0,5) has focal distances 8 and 2, summing to 10. Example F — translated ellipse. Foci (−1,−1) and (5,−1), sum 10 imply center (2,−1), c=3, a=5, b²=16; hence (x−2)²/25+(y+1)²/16=1. Example G — vertical hyperbola. Foci (0,±5), absolute difference 6 give y²/9−x²/16=1.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Task: derive the equations from the focal-distance definitions. Ellipse: Step 1: set d₁=√((x+c)²+y²), d₂=√((x−c)²+y²) and d₁+d₂=2a with a>c≥0. Step 2: since d₁²−d₂²=4cx, factor (d₁−d₂)(d₁+d₂)=4cx to obtain d₁−d₂=2cx/a. Step 3: add and subtract to obtain d₁=a+cx/a and d₂=a−cx/a. Step 4: square d₁ and simplify: (1−c²/a²)x²+y²=a²−c². Step 5: divide by b²=a²−c²>0 to get x²/a²+y²/b²=1. Hyperbola: Step 6: on the right branch use d₁−d₂=2a with 0<a<c. The same difference-of-squares relation gives d₁+d₂=2cx/a, so d₂=cx/a−a. Step 7: squaring d₂ and simplifying yields (c²/a²−1)x²−y²=c²−a². Step 8: with b²=c²−a²>0, divide to obtain x²/a²−y²/b²=1; reflection across the y-axis gives the left branch. Step 9: substitute example foci (±3,0), sum 10 to get x²/25+y²/16=1; substitute foci (±5,0), difference 6 to get x²/9−y²/16=1. Step 10: verify a vertex against each original distance condition, not only the squared equation.

 Additional source-grounded task: begin with foci (0,−3) and (0,3) and total distance 10. Step 1: midpoint is (0,0), so c=3 and the major axis is vertical. Step 2: a=5, b²=a²−c²=16. Step 3: write y²/25+x²/16=1, not x²/25+y²/16=1. Step 4: check at vertical vertex (0,5): distance to the lower focus is 8, to the upper is 2; sum 10. Step 5: shift both foci 2 units right and 1 unit down, giving (2,−4),(2,2); new equation (y+1)²/25+(x−2)²/16=1. Step 6: to construct a source-inspired string model, hold the two foci fixed, vary the constant sum and observe its effect on a and b; record distances rather than inferring equation solely from the drawing.

Accessible ellipse string/foci construction (original Edulytiks learning activity): Fix foci F₁=(−3,0), F₂=(3,0) and require the sum of distances to be 10 units. For a two-ended string attached separately to the two foci and pulled taut by a pencil, a 10-unit string corresponds directly to d(P,F₁)+d(P,F₂)=10. With a CLOSED LOOP routed around both tacks and the pencil, the return segment between the fixed tacks is 6 units, so the physical loop length is 16 units: d(P,F₁)+d(P,F₂)+d(F₁,F₂)=10+6=16. A 10-unit closed loop would instead leave distance sum 4, less than the 6-unit focus separation, and cannot trace this nondegenerate ellipse. State explicitly which physical construction is used. A student can alternatively use a coordinate grid or a table of focal distances without physical string. At (5,0) the distances are 8 and 2; at (0,4) they are 5 and 5, so both lie on x²/25+y²/16=1. At (0,5) the distances are √34 and √34, so the sum is not 10 and the point must be rejected. Describe how changing the constant sum to 12 with the foci fixed changes b² from 16 to 27, and how moving the foci to (±4,0) with sum 10 changes b² to 9. Rotate the focal axis to obtain x²/16+y²/25=1 for foci (0,±3), and translate the center to (2,−1) to obtain (x−2)²/25+(y+1)²/16=1. Separately label the constant-DIFFERENCE hyperbola with foci (±5,0) and difference 6 as an independently authored extension, not the original ellipse-string task. Teacher explanation should require the original distance definitions and nondegeneracy restrictions, not merely an equation guess.

Source 6.10H closed-loop experiment (new first-party, nonvisual alternative): Position the two tacks 4 inches apart, so focus offset c=2 inches, and make CLOSED string loops of length 10, 12 and 14 inches. When the pencil pulls each loop taut around both tacks, the return segment between fixed tacks uses 4 inches. Therefore the two free focus-to-pencil lengths have constant sums 6, 8 and 10 inches, respectively; the semimajor axes are a=3, 4 and 5 inches. The corresponding semiminor squares b²=a²−c² are 5, 12 and 21 square inches. The ellipses are x²/9+y²/5=1, x²/16+y²/12=1 and x²/25+y²/21=1. Increasing the loop length with the tacks fixed increases a. If the CLOSED loop stays 14 inches while tack separation changes from 4 to 6 inches, the free-distance sum falls from 10 to 8 and c rises from 2 to 3, so a changes to 4 and b² becomes 7. This is different from holding the free focal-distance sum constant while only changing c; the physical string definition must be stated precisely. For the 14-inch loop with foci (−2,0),(2,0), point (5,0) has distances 7 and 3, and point (0,√21) has two distances of 5, satisfying the required sum 10. Point (0,6) gives 2√40>10 and is not on the ellipse. Check these distances in the original radical expression, not by squaring blindly. Extend the explanation to vertical and shifted foci by identifying midpoint, major-axis direction, proper larger denominator and strict a>c. Label the separately taught hyperbola constant-absolute-difference derivation as an original Edulytiks CCSS extension, not an original publisher 6.10H activity. Check for understanding: give one valid/one invalid focal-distance point, compare the three closed loops, reject a=c degeneracy, and require teacher review of the string or equivalent accessible construction.
translations.commonMistakes:
Using a constant difference to define an ellipse or a constant sum to define a hyperbola. Mistaking focal separation 2c for the constant sum 2a. Interchanging b²=a²−c² (ellipse) and b²=c²−a² (hyperbola). Forgetting hyperbola focal difference is an absolute value, so two symmetric branches appear. Treating the two focal distances as signed: they are always nonnegative. Accepting 2a≤2c for a nondegenerate ellipse or 2a≥2c for a nondegenerate hyperbola. Squaring a radical equation and never checking the original condition. Giving a numerical equation with correct denominators but omitting that the foci are positioned on the x-axis.

 Assuming every ellipse with vertical foci uses x²/a² as its major-axis term; the larger denominator belongs under y² when the major axis is vertical. Forgetting the midpoint when foci are shifted: the translated center is (h,k), not always (0,0). Predicting a wider ellipse after increasing c while keeping a fixed, even though b²=a²−c² decreases. Mistaking the physical loop's total string length for the two free pencil-to-focus segments without accounting for the 6-unit segment between the fixed tacks: a 10-unit two-ended string is valid for focal sum 10, but a taut CLOSED loop must be 16 units long, not 10.
translations.quickSummary:
Ellipse: constant SUM of distances to foci (±c,0) is 2a>2c; set b²=a²−c²>0 and obtain x²/a²+y²/b²=1. Hyperbola: constant ABSOLUTE DIFFERENCE is 2a<2c; set b²=c²−a²>0 and obtain x²/a²−y²/b²=1. Derive these equations with the distance formula and algebra, then check a vertex against the original focal condition. The recorded source task primarily develops the ellipse; the hyperbola is independently authored CCSS coverage requiring its own academic source-equivalence review.

 Additional ellipse source goals: with a fixed distance sum 2a, increasing focal separation 2c makes b²=a²−c² smaller; fixing c and increasing a widens the ellipse. Vertical foci yield x²/b²+y²/a²=1, and translated foci give shifted-center terms. For vertical hyperbolas, interchange x and y in the positive-axis equation. These are first-party explanatory examples; no original copyrighted student figures are reproduced.
